section_summary: This section contains SCAP and State Department reporting on Japan’s rapidly changing postwar party system, including coalition negotiations, cabinet rumors, Communist tactics, women in politics, and a detailed survey of the minor parties represented in the 90th Diet. It also documents the appointment of Elizabeth Gray Vining as tutor to the crown prince, profiles political financier Tsuji Karoku, assesses the Japanese Communist Party, and discusses the nationality and policing of Formosans in occupied Japan. The final pages request administrative reports and list the principal officers of Japan’s six major political parties.

subfiles.title: Political Parties Semi-Monthly Report, 16–31 July 1946, concluding pages
subfiles.from: Political Parties Branch, Political Affairs Division, Government Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Reports party disputes, coalition negotiations, the creation of the Shinsei-kai, and restrictions on Communist speaking in the Diet.
subfiles.summary: The report describes rumors that Prime Minister Yoshida might resign or reorganize his cabinet, while Hatoyama continued to influence the Liberal Party informally. It analyzes a possible Progressive–Social Democratic–Co-operative coalition, concluding that disagreements over leadership, policy, and cabinet posts made it unlikely. It also profiles the newly formed Shinsei-kai and recounts Communist overuse of Diet interpellation time and disappointing Communist-supported local-election results.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of the Political Party Fortnightly Report, 16–31 July 1946
subfiles.about: Summarizes the late-July report on party realignment, constitutional work, Communist Diet restrictions, and political rumors.
subfiles.summary: The abstract notes the formation of the Shinsei-kai by minor groups and independents, giving it the procedural rights of a Diet group with more than twenty-five members. It also records restrictions on Communist speaking, rumors of Yoshida’s resignation and Liberal division, and speculation about the political return of purged leaders and new conservative alliances.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 564 forwarding the Political Parties Semi-Monthly Report, 1–15 August 1946
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards SCAP’s semi-monthly report on Japanese political parties for the first half of August 1946.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser transmits a Government Section report covering party affairs from 1 through 15 August. The despatch states that the report is adequately summarized in its opening paragraphs.

subfiles.title: Political Parties Semi-Monthly Report, 1–15 August 1946
subfiles.from: Political Affairs Division, Government Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Surveys cabinet politics, failed conservative merger talks, Socialist consolidation, centrist reorganization, Communist setbacks, women’s initiatives, and public opinion.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Yoshida’s planned inauguration as Liberal Party president, the stalemate over a Liberal–Progressive merger, and pressure to replace bureaucratic ministers with party politicians. It gives particular attention to the proposed merger of the Co-operative Democratic Party and Shinsei-kai into a new centrist party capable of holding the Diet balance of power. Other sections discuss Socialist labor support, Communist setbacks, Sano Gaku’s proposed movement for socialism under the emperor system, women’s peace and legal initiatives, and an Asahi poll showing unusually strong Socialist support.

subfiles.title: Office memorandum concerning the Stoddard–Vining file
subfiles.about: Internal correspondence concerning the Stoddard file and related material, preserved in badly garbled OCR.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum appears to thank Curran for access to a file and to discuss further handling of material concerning Stoddard. A handwritten continuation is largely illegible but belongs to the same internal exchange.

subfiles.title: Memorandum submitting draft announcement of the crown prince’s tutor
subfiles.about: Submits for approval a draft concerning the appointment of an American tutor to Japan’s crown prince.
subfiles.summary: Bowles forwards an attached draft for Curran’s approval. He explains that it follows an earlier Department press release in March concerning the search for the crown prince’s tutor.

subfiles.title: Draft press release on Elizabeth Gray Vining’s appointment
subfiles.about: Announces that the Japanese Imperial Household accepted George Stoddard’s recommendation of Elizabeth Gray Vining as tutor to the crown prince.
subfiles.summary: The draft identifies Vining as a Philadelphia Quaker, teacher, children’s author, and trained librarian. It explains that Emperor Hirohito had asked Stoddard to recommend a suitable American woman and reviews Vining’s education and teaching career. Her duties were to include both private instruction of the crown prince and teaching at the Peers’ School.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting copies of the Vining press release
subfiles.about: Sends Stoddard copies of the Department’s press release concerning Vining.
subfiles.summary: Curran explains that William Benton is out of town and encloses copies of the press release for Stoddard’s use. The brief letter is sent to Stoddard at the University of Illinois in Urbana.

subfiles.title: Telegram to George Stoddard about the press release
subfiles.about: Advises Stoddard that attempts to reach him failed and that a copy of the press release is being sent by air mail.
subfiles.summary: Curran tells Stoddard that she was unable to reach him. She states that the press release is being air-mailed that day.

subfiles.title: Urgent instruction to obtain the press release and call Stoddard
subfiles.about: Directs staff to obtain copies of the press release and place a firm telephone call to Stoddard.
subfiles.summary: The terse handwritten or typed instruction marks the matter urgent. It requests copies of the release and a confirmed call to Stoddard, with his number noted elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Routing note for the Stoddard file
subfiles.from: Office of the Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Routes attached Stoddard material within the Department of State.
subfiles.summary: The fragment identifies a Stoddard file as attached and directs it to Mr. Latimer. A handwritten instruction appears to request its return after review.

subfiles.title: Department of State Press Release No. 599: Selection of Elizabeth Gray Vining
subfiles.about: Officially announces Elizabeth Gray Vining’s selection as tutor to Japan’s crown prince.
subfiles.summary: At Stoddard’s request, Assistant Secretary William Benton discloses Vining’s selection and explains how the emperor asked the American Education Mission to find a tutor. The release summarizes Vining’s teaching, writing, and library-science background and states that she will also teach at the Peers’ School.

subfiles.title: DC/R routing slip for the Vining material
subfiles.to: Department offices listed for action or copies
subfiles.about: Records the internal distribution and routing of the Vining appointment papers.
subfiles.summary: The slip assigns action and copy destinations within the Department. It contains no substantive discussion of the appointment.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 567 forwarding a study of minor parties in the 90th Diet
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a SCAP study of the minor political parties represented in Japan’s 90th Diet.
subfiles.summary: The despatch outlines the study’s treatment of election results, post-election alignments, party objectives, representatives’ biographies, and their views on the constitution and food crisis. It notes broad support for the government constitution draft, repeated demands for fertilizer, and the report’s description of most minor-party representatives as conservative. It emphasizes the quantity of biographical intelligence in the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Minor Parties Represented in the 90th Diet, with annex on twenty-three parties
subfiles.from: Political Parties Branch, Public Administration Division, Government Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Analyzes minor-party election results and alignments and supplies profiles of twenty-three parties and their Diet representatives.
subfiles.summary: The study explains that only twenty-five minor parties elected members in April 1946 and that most of their representatives were soon absorbed into major parties or the Independent Club and Shinsei-kai. It characterizes their organizations as small, weakly disciplined, conservative, opportunistic, or tied to particular interests, while noting some sincere reformers. The annex gives each party’s leadership, membership, objectives, election results, affiliations, and representatives’ views on the constitution, food, women’s rights, labor, local government, land reform, bureaucracy, and reconstruction. Recurring proposals include increased fertilizer production, higher rice prices, improved distribution, food imports through SCAP, preservation of the emperor system, and expansion of women’s legal and economic rights.

subfiles.title: DC/R routing slip for Despatch No. 567
subfiles.to: Department offices listed for action or copies
subfiles.about: Records the internal distribution of the despatch and study on minor parties.
subfiles.summary: The routing slip identifies Tokyo Despatch No. 567 and lists offices receiving action or information copies. It contains no additional substantive analysis.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 568 transmitting a pen portrait of Tsuji Karoku
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits Harry Emerson Wildes’s biographical and political profile of Tsuji Karoku.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser forwards a pen portrait prepared by Wildes, Assistant Chief of SCAP’s Political Affairs Division. The enclosure is identified as a memorandum on Tsuji Karoku.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Record: Tsuji Karoku
subfiles.from: Harry Emerson Wildes, Political Affairs Division, SCAP
subfiles.about: Profiles Tsuji Karoku’s career as a political financier, contractor, adventurer, and informal broker of influence.
subfiles.summary: Wildes depicts Tsuji as a small, enigmatic figure who financed candidates from 1920 onward while claiming that gratitude was his only desired return. The profile traces his early activities in China and Formosa, his return to Tokyo, his party connections, and allegations that he used visiting cards and personal access to advance business or political interests. Tsuji denied seeking contracts or wielding political power, but the memorandum presents him as an enduring behind-the-scenes operator linked to controversial transactions and politicians.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of the Tsuji Karoku pen portrait
subfiles.about: Summarizes Wildes’s report on Tsuji Karoku’s political history and current influence.
subfiles.summary: The abstract describes the enclosure as a Government Section account of Tsuji’s history and present activities. It notes allegations that Tsuji influenced politicians while they held office.

subfiles.title: Duplicate departmental abstract of the Tsuji Karoku pen portrait
subfiles.about: Duplicate abstract describing Wildes’s report on Tsuji Karoku.
subfiles.summary: This page substantially duplicates the preceding abstract. It again characterizes the Wildes report as an account of Tsuji’s history, current political position, and influence over officeholders.

subfiles.title: Moscow Embassy comments on SCAP’s study of the Japanese Communist Party
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, with copy to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Comments on SCAP’s July 1946 paper concerning Japanese Communist strategy and its possible dependence on Moscow.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy contrasts the initially militant line of Tokuda and Shiga, imprisoned since the 1920s, with the gradualist tactics brought back by Nozaka after years in Moscow and Yan’an. It argues that the party is clearly seeking power but that the degree of subservience to Moscow is harder to prove, suggesting investigation of Nozaka’s Yan’an associates, Soviet-returned Japanese, and the party’s alignment with Soviet foreign-policy positions. The despatch recommends fostering a strong economy and liberal movement while permitting Japanese democrats to publish accurate information about conditions in the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 402 on the treatment and nationality of Formosans in Japan
subfiles.about: Requests policy review concerning Formosan nationality, policing, repatriation, and Chinese diplomatic protection in occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson reports that roughly 100,000 Formosans in Japan were viewed by occupation authorities as an unruly element heavily involved in black-market activity and violent clashes with Japanese police. He explains that Chinese claims of nationality and diplomatic protection had created uncertainty over arrest, trial, repatriation, welfare responsibility, and jurisdiction because no Chinese occupation courts existed. After discussions with Ambassador Chu Shih-Ming, Atcheson concluded that China lacked definite repatriation and support plans. He asks SCAP and the Department to reconsider whether all Formosans should be treated as United Nations nationals exempt from ordinary Japanese police authority.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 424 requesting an urgent reply on the Formosan problem
subfiles.about: Urgently requests the Department’s response to the earlier telegram on Formosans in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson states that the Formosan problem is becoming more aggravated each day. He asks for the Department’s comments on Telegram No. 402 as soon as possible and references related communications with Nanjing.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2021 requesting monthly summaries of nonmilitary activities in Tokyo
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Requests regular copies of the military authorities’ monthly summary of nonmilitary activities in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The London Embassy understands that American military authorities prepare a monthly summation of nonmilitary activities in Tokyo. It asks that copies be supplied to the Embassy each month if possible.

subfiles.title: Memorandum forwarding London’s request for Tokyo activity summaries
subfiles.from: J. D. Beal, Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.to: Lieutenant Colonel Charles B. Smith, War Department
subfiles.about: Asks the War Department to provide copies of the military’s Tokyo nonmilitary-activity summaries for transmission to London.
subfiles.summary: Beal forwards a copy of London Despatch No. 2021 and repeats the Embassy’s understanding that U.S. military authorities issue a monthly nonmilitary summary. He asks that the material be supplied for onward transmission to the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 650 transmitting a list of principal political-party officers
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a list of the principal officers of Japan’s six major political parties.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser encloses a roster of senior officers in the six major Japanese parties. He states that a more detailed report on political parties will follow in the near future.

subfiles.title: Principal officers of the six major political parties in Japan
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Lists the leadership and principal committees of Japan’s Social Democratic, Liberal, Progressive, Communist, Co-operative Democratic, and National parties.
subfiles.summary: The roster identifies party presidents or chief secretaries, executive and general-affairs committees, managers, political-research officials, accountants, advisers, and Diet caucus officers. It records Yoshida Shigeru as Liberal president, Shidehara Kijuro as Progressive president, the Japanese Communist Central Committee headed by figures including Tokuda, Shiga, and Nozaka, and Yamamoto Sanehiko and Ikawa Tadao as leading Co-operative Democratic officials. The National Party list continues through the end of this section.
